title: The foolishness of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18–25)
hook: the foolishness of God is wiser than men

segments.voice: Yesterday, the living sacrifice of Romans 12. Your line was rejoice and weep with them. Whose room did you walk into? Day five hundred sixty-nine.

On the Palatine Hill in Rome, archaeologists found a scratched drawing on a plaster wall, probably from around the year two hundred. It shows a figure on a cross with the head of a donkey, and a young man raising a hand toward it. Underneath, in rough Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. It's a joke, a schoolboy's mockery of a Christian. It's also one of the oldest surviving pictures of the crucifixion. And Paul would not have been surprised by it at all.
screen: `A SCRATCH ON A ROMAN WALL.` → `A CRUCIFIED FIGURE, MOCKED.` → `ALEXAMENOS WORSHIPS HIS GOD.`

segments.voice: We're turning now to Paul's letters to Corinth, a rich, proud, quarrelsome port city. The church there is splitting into fan clubs, and some members prize clever speech and wisdom. So Paul starts at the hardest point. In the King James: "For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God." The Greek word for foolishness is moria. Our word moron comes from the same family. Paul is saying: yes, to many people, this sounds moronic. A crucified Messiah. A God who wins by losing. Crucifixion was Rome's death for slaves and rebels. You didn't mention it at dinner. Paul knows how it sounds to the people around him. To some, a stumbling block; to others, foolishness. He doesn't make it sound more respectable. Instead he turns it around: "Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Then, with a smile, he tells the Corinthians to look at themselves: not many of you were wise by worldly standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth. God chose what the world counts foolish and weak. The mocking drawing on the wall and Paul's letter agree on one thing: from the outside, the cross looks absurd. Paul's claim is that the absurd thing is exactly where God chose to show his power. Catholics place the crucifix at the center of every church, over the altar, the very image the mockers drew, now held up without embarrassment.
screen: `CORINTH, PROUD OF ITS WISDOM.` · `MORIA: FOOLISHNESS.` · `A GOD WHO WINS BY LOSING.` · `NOT MANY WISE, NOT MANY MIGHTY.` · then, large: `THE FOOLISHNESS OF GOD IS WISER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one foolish kindness. Settle, and breathe. Think of something kind that would look a little silly or pointless by the world's math. Letting someone have the parking spot. Paying for the coffee behind you. Spending a long time with someone who can't do anything for you. Forgiving a debt, small or large. Picture doing it, and picture someone shaking their head. Let that be fine. If you pray, you can look at a crucifix or picture one, and remember how foolish it looked. The bell holds the time.
The foolishness of the cross. A crucified Messiah, mocked as absurd, and Paul's claim that God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: foolish and wise. Today, do one kind thing that doesn't make sense on paper. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholic churches place a crucifix on or near the altar, Catholics often wear or hang one at home, and on Good Friday the faithful come forward to venerate the cross.

fork.setup: you're Paul. the church in Corinth prizes clever speech, and your message centers on an execution. where do you start?
options: with the cross itself, admitting how foolish it sounds.
fork.reveal: he starts at the hardest point: the preaching of the cross is foolishness to some, but to us the power of God.

original.note: Greek: foolishness, folly. the same family as our word moron.

trapdoor: what you thought: the cross was always a respected religious symbol.
what it means: in Paul's world it was a mark of total shame, and he says God chose exactly that to show his power and wisdom.
what a scholar hears: Christians seldom depicted the crucifixion in art until about the fifth century. one of the earliest images is the mocking Alexamenos graffito from the Palatine.

notes: Confirm KJV wording of 1 Corinthians 1:18 and 1:25.

Verse 1:23 ('unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness') is deliberately paraphrased as 'to some, a stumbling block; to others, foolishness' to avoid any framing against Jewish listeners; a Keeper may prefer the full verse.
Alexamenos graffito: dates proposed range from the late 1st to the early 3rd century; 'probably around the year two hundred' hedged. Confirm.
Moron from Greek mōros: standard etymology; confirm.
Crucifixion rarely depicted before the 5th century (e.g. Santa Sabina doors): confirm.
